subject: Archaeology
title: When Digging Is Not Allowed
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: When Digging Is Not Allowed.

hook.text: Sometimes the best archaeology means not digging at all. Many sacred and sensitive sites must be left alone.

buildup.text: Indigenous communities worldwide have fought to protect burial grounds and sacred places from excavation.

discovery.text: Non-invasive methods like GPR, magnetometry, and satellite imaging can study sites without disturbing the ground.

twist.text: NAGPRA, the U.S. law passed in 1990, requires museums to return Native American remains and sacred objects to tribes.

climax.text: More archaeologists now consult communities before digging. The field shifted from 'right to dig' to 'permission to dig.'

punchline.text: Science does not always have the right to dig.

quiz.question: What does NAGPRA require U.S. museums to do?
options: Pay royalties to tribes for displaying Native American artifacts
Return Native American remains and sacred objects to tribes
Fund archaeological surveys on all tribal lands

details.summary: Many archaeological sites cannot be excavated due to sacred status, private ownership, urban development, political restrictions, or preservation policies. Non-invasive techniques — geophysics, satellite survey, surface collection, and historical research — allow study without breaking ground.
details.whyItMatters: Excavation is not always possible, ethical, or necessary. Non-invasive methods can answer research questions while preserving sites intact for future generations with better technology and different questions.
takeaways: Many sites cannot be dug due to legal or ethical restrictions
Non-invasive methods study sites without excavation
Preserving sites intact saves them for future research

faq.question: What non-invasive methods can study sites without digging?
faq.answer: Ground-penetrating radar and magnetometry map buried features. Satellite and aerial imagery detect surface traces. Surface collection gathers exposed artifacts. LiDAR reveals topographic features. eDNA from surface soil can identify past occupants.

faq.question: Why do some archaeologists advocate not digging at all?
faq.answer: Since excavation destroys what it studies, some argue that current questions don't justify the permanent loss. Future technologies may extract far more information from intact deposits. Selective excavation — digging only what is needed to answer specific questions
